summary: Describes a YANG data model for managing the Routing Information Protocol, covering both RIP version 2 and RIPng. It includes configuration, operational state, and remote procedure calls, and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

eli5.summary: RIP is an old way for routers to share maps. This gives a standard form to set up and inspect it on a device.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring RIPv2 and RIPng and reading their state from a router.

tldr.problem: Every vendor exposed RIP settings and state in its own way, so network management tools could not configure or monitor RIP on different devices in a uniform manner.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8695 defines the YANG module ietf-rip. It augments the core routing model with a rip container holding configuration, operational state and one RPC, clear-rip-route, and it covers both RIP version 2 and RIPng.
tldr.outcome: Tools that speak NETCONF or RESTCONF can manage RIP through one shared schema. The model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture, and it is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8695 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What the Data Model Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8695 introduces a YANG data model for the Routing Information Protocol (RIP). RIP was designed to work as an Interior Gateway Protocol in moderate-size Autonomous Systems. The model supports both RIP version 2, defined in RFC 2453 and carrying IPv4, and RIPng, defined in RFC 2080 and carrying IPv6.

A device that implements RIP version 2 or RIPng can use the model to configure the protocol, manage its operational behaviors and retrieve its operational status. The capabilities described in RFC 1724, the RIP version 2 MIB extension, are covered.
sections.eli5: RIP is a way for routers to tell each other where things are. This document is a standard checklist for setting up and checking a router's RIP.

sections.title: Where RIP Fits in the Routing Model
sections.content:
The module augments the core routing data model ietf-routing from RFC 8349. Under routing/control-plane-protocols/control-plane-protocol it adds a rip container. That container instantiates one RIP entity, which supports either RIP version 2 or RIPng. Depending on how ietf-routing is implemented, a RIP instance MAY belong to a logical router or network instance.

Inside the container, configuration is organized around three entities: the protocol instance, the interface and the neighbor. Each interface is referenced by name from the ietf-interfaces model, and each interface can hold a list of explicitly configured neighbors.
sections.eli5: Think of a big filing cabinet for router settings. This model adds one new drawer labeled RIP, with folders for the whole router, each network port and each neighbor.

sections.title: Configuration Knobs
sections.content:
Per-instance settings include a default metric, an administrative distance (default 120), maximum-paths for load balancing over equal-cost routes (default 8), a triggered-update-threshold and an output-delay between packets of a multipacket update. A redistribute container can pull in routes from BGP, IS-IS, OSPFv2, OSPFv3, other RIP instances, connected and static routes, and several other sources, each with an optional metric and route policy.

Four timers control the protocol, in seconds. The update-interval defaults to 30, the invalid-interval to 180 (at least three times the update interval), the holddown-interval to 180 and the flush-interval to 240 (larger than the invalid interval).

Per interface, the model offers authentication (a key chain or a key with a crypto algorithm), BFD, a cost, passive (stop sending) and no-listen (stop listening), a summary-address and split-horizon. Split horizon can be disabled, simple (the default) or poison-reverse.
sections.eli5: These are the dials on the router. How often to shout updates, how long to wait before deciding a neighbor went quiet, and whether to repeat news back to the neighbor who told you.

sections.title: State, the RPC and Notifications
sections.content:
Operational state sits beside configuration in the same hierarchy, as the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342 expects. When state is read from the operational datastore, the result covers both read-write (config true) and read-only (config false) nodes. State can be retrieved at the levels of protocol instance, interface, neighbor and route, with separate ipv4 and ipv6 neighbor and route tables. Optional statistics count requests and responses globally, and bad packets, bad routes and updates sent per interface.

The model defines exactly one RPC, clear-rip-route, which clears RIP routes from the routing table. It defines no RIP-specific notifications; the mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641 can be used to subscribe, filter and receive periodic or on-demand updates.
sections.eli5: Besides settings, you can ask the router what it currently knows: its neighbors, its routes and some counts. There is also one button that says forget the RIP routes.

sections.title: Optional Features
sections.content: Some parts of the model are beyond basic RIP and are guarded by YANG features. The module defines bfd, explicit-neighbors, global-statistics and interface-statistics. Each vendor decides whether to support a given feature on a device. Explicit neighbors are described as useful for a non-broadcast multiple access (NBMA) network.
sections.eli5: Not every router has every extra gadget, so the model lets a router say which extras it has and skip the others.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. The mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM) can limit which users may reach which parts.

Writing to the rip subtree without protection can affect the routing subsystem of the device and the network, leading to malfunctions or packets delivered to inappropriate destinations. Reading it can disclose the operational state of RIP on the device. The clear-rip-route RPC carries the same kind of risk, so access to it should be controlled.
sections.eli5: Whoever can change a router's routing settings can mess up the whole network, so only trusted people should get the keys.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-rip in the IETF XML Registry. It also registers the module ietf-rip, with prefix rip, in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: The module gets its official name entered in the public list of names, so nobody else uses it.

items.label: update-interval
items.desc: How often RIP updates are sent.

items.label: invalid-interval
items.desc: Time without updates before a route is declared invalid.

items.label: holddown-interval
items.desc: Time before better routes are released.

items.label: flush-interval
items.desc: Time before a route is flushed from the routing table.
